prompt.context: Minerva's University Fluids Research Lab has discovered a more efficient way to transport crude petroleum oil inside pipelines. This new technology can be used in midstream applications where the oil is acquired from the extraction plant and delivered to the refinery plant. The university invested $1,200M in this project during the last 12 years. The new technology mixes water and oil under certain conditions to reduce the loss of energy caused by the friction between the oil and the pipeline surface while being transported. As a result, the transport between two given points gets 15% faster and the useful lifetime of the pipelines increases by 20%. Minerva's University has asked our help to value for how much they should sell the technology.
prompt.question: How much should Minerva's University sell this new pipeline oil technology for?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors and what is their market share?
clarifying_info.a: National Oil Company (NOC) is the only player. However, the market is open for the last two years.
Primarily NOC. However, two other prospects are also interested in entering the market.

clarifying_info.q: Does the university have a patent? How long does it last?
clarifying_info.a: The university has already filed the patent, which lasts for 20 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is NOC's current pipeline capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Full capacity. Surplus is transported by more expensive means such as rail car, barge, and truck.

clarifying_info.q: How is the demand for crude oil?
clarifying_info.a: NOC sells all the crude oil it buys. See Exhibit 2 for the next years forecast.

clarifying_info.q: Can NOC build more pipelines to substitute other means of transportation?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, it is an alternative. However, there are costs involved. Additional capacity: 50,000 barrels per day; time to implement: 2 years; cost per additional capacity: $700M.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to implement this technology?
clarifying_info.a: Minerva's University estimates that the technology would be running in 100% of the pipelines in one year at $2,000M installation cost.

exhibits.title: Income Statement and Cost of Sales Breakdown
exhibits.shows: Table 1 shows the income statement for Year 0 assuming sales of 2M barrels per day. Table 2 shows the cost of sales breakdown per means of transportation.

exhibits.title: Crude Oil Demand Forecast
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the crude oil demand forecast in millions of barrels per day over 20 years. Demand starts at approximately 2M barrels/day and rises linearly to approximately 2.5M barrels/day by year 20.

data.note: In a given year, demand per day is equal for all 360 days.

framework: A) Pricing: Value = (1) Savings in Cost of Transportation + (2) Savings in Cost of Replacing Pipelines - (3) Cost to Implement
(1) Savings in Cost of Transportation: increased pipeline flow speed raises delivery capacity; saves cost by switching volume from expensive means (truck, rail) to pipeline
(2) Savings in Cost of Replacing Pipelines: longer pipeline lifetime (20% increase) reduces replacement frequency and cost
B) Comparison: validate pricing against two benchmarks
(4) Research Investment by Minerva's University: $1,200M — sets the floor (university must at least recover its investment)
(5) Alternative Investment for NOC: cost to expand pipeline network — sets the ceiling (NOC will not pay more than the cost of its next-best alternative)

questions.prompt: Calculate the Savings in Cost of Transportation (SCOT) over 20 years (the patent lifetime).
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that (a) the 15% speed increase allows more volume through existing pipelines, freeing capacity currently handled by truck and rail; and (b) the per-barrel cost savings from switching those volumes to pipeline can be quantified. Key insight: pipeline capacity increase = 15% speed gain × 70% current pipeline share ≈ 10.5% ≈ 10% additional pipeline use. That 10% volume was previously split among truck (5%) and rail (5%).

math.setup:
SCOT = Total Sales over 20 years × Savings per barrel from switching
Total Sales (trapezoid area under demand curve) × 360 days × $10/barrel
Savings per barrel = % switch to pipeline × (cost differential per mode)
steps: Total Sales over 20 years = trapezoid area × 360 days × $10/barrel
Trapezoid area (millions of barrels/day × years) = [(2 + 2.5) × 20 × 0.5] = 45 million barrels-years
Pipeline capacity increase = 15% speed gain × 70% current share = 10.5% ≈ 10%
Switching sources: truck 5%, rail 5% (total 10% = the newly freed capacity)

questions.prompt: Calculate the Savings in Cost of Replacing Pipelines (SCRP) over 20 years.
questions.guidance: The 20% increase in pipeline lifetime means pipelines last longer, reducing replacement frequency. Candidate should identify current replacement cost, current lifetime, and new lifetime to compute the saving.

math.setup: SCRP = Annual replacement cost × 20 years × (1 - new lifetime / current lifetime)
steps: Current cost of replacing pipelines = $1,000M/year (from Exhibit 1)
Note: casebook uses 5-year vs 4-year replacement cycle interpretation: new lifetime factor expressed as 1 - 4/5 = 0.20

questions.prompt: What is the net value of the technology to NOC, and what is the pricing range?
questions.guidance: Candidate should subtract the installation cost from the gross savings to get net value. Then bracket the price between the university's floor (R&D investment) and NOC's ceiling (net savings or alternative investment cost).

math.setup:
Net value = SCOT + SCRP - Installation cost
Floor = Minerva's R&D investment
Ceiling = min(Net value to NOC, Alternative investment)
steps: Less installation cost = $10,000M - $2,000M = $8,000M net value to NOC
University floor: $1,200M (must at least recover R&D)
NOC ceiling from net savings: NOC will pay up to $8,000M
NOC will prefer buying the technology over expanding the network if price < $7,000M

questions.prompt: Calculate the alternative investment cost if NOC were to expand its pipeline network instead of buying the technology.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute how many incremental 50,000-barrel/day tranches are needed to go from 2M to 2.5M barrels/day, then multiply by cost per tranche.

math.setup: Alternative investment = (Required additional capacity / Capacity per unit) × Cost per unit

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or sensitive assumptions should Minerva's University consider before finalizing the pricing and negotiation strategy?

categories.name: Implementation risks
ideas: Delay in the installation of the new technology beyond the estimated one year
High upfront installation cost of $2,000M — NOC may require financing support (cash surplus, bank loan, equity increase)
Technical challenges in achieving full 100% pipeline coverage

categories.name: Market and demand risks
ideas: Crude oil demand changes due to economic crisis, energy transition, or geopolitical factors
Crude oil price fluctuation — use futures contracts to guarantee buying and selling prices
NOC may negotiate aggressively given it is the dominant player

categories.name: Operational and geographic risks
ideas: Limitation in reaching some regions that can only be served by a specific means of transportation
Assumption that 15% speed increase translates directly to 10% additional pipeline capacity may not hold under all conditions

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: Two other prospects interested in the market could create competitive tension but also alternative negotiation leverage
Patent duration of 20 years is finite — technology could be reverse-engineered or superseded after expiry

recommendation: Sell the technology for $1,500M upfront plus a 30% participation in the additional revenue generated while the patent holds (approximately $3,000M over 20 years at 30% of $10,000M gross savings), for a total expected value of ~$4,500M
This price is above the university's floor ($1,200M R&D cost) and well below NOC's ceiling ($7,000M alternative investment), making it a compelling proposition for both parties
The technology should be positioned as superior to the pipeline expansion alternative: it deploys in 1 year vs. 2 years for new pipelines, and delivers $500M more in net savings
risks: Crude oil price fluctuations could reduce NOC's willingness to pay
Demand slowdown could erode the projected $6,000M transportation savings
Installation delays would reduce the net value and weaken the university's negotiating position
NOC may prefer the pipeline expansion alternative if financing costs are favourable
next_steps: Validate assumptions and calculations with NOC's own operational data
Define a structured negotiation strategy with clear walk-away price ($1,200M) and target price ($4,500M–$5,000M)
If negotiations with NOC fail, approach the two other prospects entering the market
Explore risk-sharing deal structures (upfront + royalty) to bridge valuation gaps
